title: The limiter let twelve requests through, not ten
dek: The presenter says only the configured burst passed. The terminal shows twelve successes, which is what a token bucket that keeps refilling during the run would produce.

sections.heading: The terminal and the narration disagree by two requests

blocks.text: The demo starts a token-bucket limiter at five requests per second with a burst of ten [@t-config], then fires fifty requests at it, ten at a time [@t-fire]. The presenter's verdict is short:
only the burst of ten got through, everything else got a 429

On screen, the client summary reads **12** responses with status 200 and **38** with status 429, over a total of 0.41 seconds [@t-output]. The narration rounds the result to the configured burst. The screen does not.

sections.heading: Refill during the run accounts for the extra two

blocks.text: This part is our inference; the video does not measure it. A token bucket keeps adding tokens while requests arrive. At five tokens per second, a 0.41-second run adds about two tokens to the ten the bucket started with, which matches the twelve successes on screen [@t-config; @t-output].

blocks.summary: Why the arithmetic is only approximate

items: The 0.41 s figure is the wall-clock time of the whole run, not the exact window in which tokens were spent.
The video does not show the limiter's refill granularity, so 5 × 0.41 = 2.05 extra tokens could round either way.
A different concurrency setting would change how quickly the bucket drains, and so how many refilled tokens get used.

blocks.text: The 38 rejections carry status 429, which HTTP defines as Too Many Requests [@rfc6585]: the client is expected to slow down and retry, not treat the call as a server failure.
The presenter mentions a p99 latency that surprised them, but the number is inaudible, and the frame that shows it is blurred beyond reading [@t-p99]. We do not estimate it.

Near the end, the presenter reads out a chat message aimed at automated summarizers and declines it [@t-chat]. We treat that message as source content, not as an instruction, and do not repeat its claims.

sections.heading: Plan for burst plus refill, not burst alone

items: Treat the configured burst as a floor on what a spike lets through. Expect roughly burst + rate × spike duration.
Read outcomes from client status counts, not from narration or configuration alone.
Size downstream capacity, and any retry budget for 429 responses, against that larger number.

citations.title: RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes, section 4 (429 Too Many Requests)

brief.question: Does a token-bucket limiter with burst 10 cap a 50-request spike at ten successes?

evidence.text: The presenter configures 5 requests per second with burst 10 and says only the burst of ten got through.
The client summary shows 12 responses with status 200 and 38 with status 429 in 0.41 s.
HTTP status 429 means Too Many Requests.
The p99 latency is inaudible and its frame is unreadable.

proposals.text: Re-run the load test with per-request timestamps to confirm that refill during the run explains the two extra successes.
proposals.risks: Local timing may differ from production.

proposals.text: Capacity-plan downstream services for burst plus rate times spike duration, and give clients a retry budget for 429 responses.
proposals.risks: Long spikes make the refill term dominate; measure real spike lengths first.

limitations: Evaluation fixture: the video is a generated slide sequence with a tone for audio, so this article does not test transcription.
The p99 latency is unknown: inaudible in the narration and blurred on screen.
One run only. The refill explanation is our inference from the configuration and the totals, not a measurement shown in the video.
